The Ambassador in Saudi Arabia (Wadsworth) to the Department of State

div.head:
No. 929
The Ambassador in Saudi Arabia (Wadsworth) to the Department of State
div.p:
Top Secret
No. 100
Ref: CA–3378, November 22, 1954

The Embassy’s views covering the feasibility of undertaking steps at this time designed to bring about an Arab-Israel settlement are forwarded in accordance with the request made in reference airgram.

Before actually tackling the problem of peace between the Arabs and the Israelis, every effort should be made to create a more favorable atmosphere. Any premature effort to seek a peace could conceivably touch off a fatal chain reaction of opposition. By creating an atmosphere of receptivity based on confidence in our general area objectives, we might eventually move the Arabs from their present intransigent position.

With regard to any approach to the problem it might be noted, by way of precedent, that there are still traces of bitterness in the U.S. between fellow American citizens over the civil war which ended nearly one hundred years ago. If the universal prosperity and opportunity in America have not been sufficient to heal the
civil war wounds in a century, surely it is expecting too much that the Arabs and Jews will be able truly to bury the hatchet in the underdeveloped Near East in less than a decade. The most that can be hoped for in the foreseeable future is an uneasy modus vivendi by whatever name it be called.

Through 1948 the large powers dealt exclusively with the Arab leaders in an effort to reach a peaceful settlement of the Palestine issue. They failed. Today the entire situation has changed; a new force—i.e. the masses—has emerged which must be reckoned with in any attempt to solve either the general problem or that of the refugees.

Not only does bitterness lie deep in the hearts of the one million refugees, who have lost confidence in the U.N., the U.S., the U.K., and in their own Arab leaders, but those leaders themselves, once in a position to impose their will on the masses, also find this no longer possible. Today the U.S. must seek the support of the masses as a prerequisite to Arab-Israeli peace.

Thus rather than embarking on the time table outlined in reference airgram, it appears that the soundest approach would be to pursue a course designed to counteract the suspicions in the minds of the Arabs regarding U.S. aims and intentions, as well as its commitments to its principal allies, Britain and France, in and with respect to the Near East. Continued demonstration of our good intentions—e.g. our determination to treat Israel as just another state in the Near East—will help to create the required favorable atmosphere without which the seeking of specific objectives will be futile.

The degree to which the inducements described in reference airgram will enable us to prepare the population for a final settlement will largely depend on the extent to which we carry out our present policy of impartiality. Various degrees of economic, technical, and military assistance together with border security (Tripartite Declaration of 1950) have already been offered to the Arabs. Although such aid has been accepted in some cases, the familiar chant still rings in our ears that the U.S. cannot “buy the Arab support” with money alone.

It is believed, therefore, that, rather than risk refusal of premature peace overtures—something we can ill afford to do—emphasis at this time should be placed on creating the atmosphere of confidence and receptivity discussed above.
The Sauds of Arabia are possessed of an adamant and long-standing hatred toward Zionism. There is nothing which suggests in the slightest a diminishing of this feeling.

The late King Abdul Aziz had no doubts about the absolute in-compatibility of his principles and Zionism. He made this clear in
1938 to H. St. Philby who had posed the hypothetical question: What would the King do if Great Britain created a Jewish state and asked him to recognize it?

“The answer”, Philby reports His Majesty as saying, “is obvious and very simple. If the Arabs—and there are many—refused to recognize the Jewish state, I, obviously, would be at their side. If, on the contrary, all of them recognized it, I, even if I were alone, would remain faithful to my opinions. The recognition of a Jewish state would be against my religion and my interests.”

The late King’s son and successor, Saud, is inbued with the same implacable feeling of opposition, intensified by the bitterness of the developments of recent years. In his speech of March 7 at the inaugural meeting of the Council of Ministers, he reminded his people: “All of us know that a cancer was established in the body of the Arab states . . . That cancer is the Zionist Jews.”

Crown Prince Faisal, who shares the King’s bitterness and singleness of purpose, asked the Ambassador in a private conversation on December 4: “Why don’t you let the Arabs and the Jews settle the Palestine problem themselves?” Asked, in reply, if he was referring to the United Nations, he answered: “Yes, if the United Nations would let us settle it between ourselves.”

With regard to the involvement of the U.N. and the Western nations in the Palestine problem, it is apparent that King Saud has little or no confidence that their efforts will satisfy the Arab view of justice.

In the King’s speech of November 12, which marked the first anniversary of his accession to the throne, he warned “those who have created this harmful disease (Israel) in the body of the Arab nation” that any remedy should not include “efforts to make peace between Arabs and Zionists . . . (which) cannot be realized.”

The King and his government can conceive of peace between Arabs and Jews in Palestine, but are aware that their conception of peace—in substance a reunited Arab Palestine—is not within grasp at the present time.

In his public statement of September 7 to Mr. Alfred Lilienthal, the King described the conditions under which it would be possible to re-establish a state of affairs such as prevailed among Arabs and Jews “before and at the start of the British Mandate in Palestine.”
1) “Return all the Palestine refugees to their homes, farms, and shops;
2) “Compensate them for all the things the Zionists caused to be spoiled, lost, ruined, or stolen;

3) “Force the Zionists to carry out all United Nations decisions concerning the Palestine case; (Comment: It is difficult to reconcile this point with the King’s reference to conditions before and during the early days of the Mandate.)
4) “Stop immediately the flow of Zionist immigration to this narrow strip of the Arab land.”

Analysis of the political, economic and social conditions of Saudi Arabia fails to disclose any readily available elements or factors which could be exploited with a view to establishing a basis for final settlement between the Arabs and Israelis.

King Saud, who is emerging in the eyes of the masses as the leading defender of Islam, has pledged himself to use every available weapon to get rid of “the cancer in the body of the Arabs”. Because of his uncompromising hostility to Zionism and his oft repeated promises in this vein, it is at present writing impossible to envisage his neutrality, let alone support, to attain peace.
In Saudi Arabia there are at best three elements worthy of consideration for exploitation purposes. These springboards are:
1) As the protector of the Moslem shrines, Saud accepts as axiomatic his special responsibility to undertake whatever is good for Islam.

In his special capacity as guardian of Mecca and Medina, it is logically conceivable that he might eventually be brought to realize that repatriating and resettling the largely Moslem refugees within favorably-adjusted Palestine frontiers and elsewhere in the Moslem World, and replacing the present unstable truce by an internationally-recognized peace settlement, would be to the overall interest of Islam as well as secure the Haram ash Sharif for the Moslems instead of exposing it to a fate similar to that of the Wailing Wall.
2) It is to Saud’s personal advantage to take every step possible to increase the stability of his monarchy.

In this connection, we should continuously stress that the U.S. has consistently supported the Saud dynasty over the years. Then, by citing the coups in Egypt, Syria and Lebanon and by calling attention to the recent events in Bahrain and the fact that elements are developing in Saudi Arabia which might eventually jeopardize the security of his throne, we might bring him to realize that he must have our support and backing in order to retain his power. From this point, he should be led to believe that by joining with us in reducing tension in the Holy Land, he would by the same stroke increase his prestige and the stability of his monarchy.
3) Saud’s tolerance regarding Christianity and Judaism (as opposed to Zionism).

Because Jerusalem is sui generis, world wide spiritual forces could be brought to bear to seek, find and implement an international solution of the problem of its future apart from general settlement of the Palestine problem.
During his meeting with Lilienthal, Saud distinguished between Judaism and Zionism and stated, “we . . . fight only Zionists. . . .”

Earlier in 1954 Saud met with five Christians and one Moslem, members of the Moral Re-Armament movement, and disclosed a strong interest in the program which stresses moral values and de-emphasizes materialism. By turning first to the Jerusalem problem and placing stress on its spiritual aspects, it may be possible to enlist Saud’s support for cooperation between Moslems and Christians first in the solution of that problem and, eventually, in the solution of the major problem of Palestine.

The above clearly shows the Saudi leaders’ deep feeling of antagonism toward Israel. Their rigid attitude provides little area for compromise. They reject peace, and, as Saudi Arabia’s concern with most of the specific problems involved (border rectifications, refugees, Jordan Valley development, etc.) is indirect, there is no real compulsion on its leaders to compromise for settlement of any of these points.
